p.seg: On the *xīnsì* day of the sixth month,
he arrived at Yúlǐng.
Because Sǎogǔ, a native of Xiálài County, illegally oppressed the people,
he was dismembered.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Emperor ascended Dū'ān Shān,
and, stroking the ruins of his ancestor Qíshǒu Kèhán,
he walked around, gazed, and sighed.
Hearing that the prison official Nièlǐ arbitrarily fabricated serious charges,
making people suffer intolerably,
some even to death,
he ordered him executed.
On the *rénchén* day,
he encamped at Lánghé,
where he captured the rebel leaders Yǎlǐ and Mílǐ,
and buried them alive beneath the south track of Tónghé.
He released the captives to return,
but many were plundered by Yúgǔlǐ.
The Emperor was enraged,
and led light cavalry to swiftly attack them.
He then dispatched brave generals to pursue and attack them via separate routes,
capturing all their followers and the plunderers.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
he encamped at Ādūn Luò.
Because his adopted son Nièlǐsī rebelled with his younger brothers,
he was shot and killed with a "ghost arrow".
The other six thousand members of his faction
were sentenced according to the severity of their crimes.
Thirty-odd captives taken by Yújué
were also allowed to atone for their crimes
and released back to their own tribes.
Arriving west of Shílǐng,
an imperial edict ordered the collection of weapons abandoned by the returning army due to lack of provisions,
and summoned the northern armies to verify and return them.
Because Yílírjǐn Nièlǐgǔn sided with his younger brothers in rebellion,
the Emperor could not bear to execute him publicly,
and ordered him to throw himself off a cliff to his death.
In the eighth month, autumn, on the *jǐmǎo* day,
he visited Lóngméi Gōng.
Twenty-nine members of the rebel faction were dismembered by carts.
Their wives and daughters were bestowed upon meritorious generals and officers.
The plundered treasures and livestock were returned to their owners;
for those whose original possessions were lost,
he ordered their families to compensate.
Those who could not compensate
were given their former subordinates.
On the *rénxū* day of the ninth month,
the Emperor departed from Xīlóu.
In the tenth month, winter, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
he was stationed at Chìyá.
On the *wùyín* day,
the Huíhú of Hézhōu came to pay tribute.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
Dílǐgǔ of the Yǐshì Fǔ and Tèlǐ of the Mígǔlí tribe were executed for their involvement in the rebellion.
An imperial edict commanded the ministers to resolve outstanding lawsuits,
with Hán Zhīgǔ recording the proceedings
and Zhīlǐgū in charge of apprehending fugitives.
In the eleventh month,
sacrifices were offered at Mùyè Shān.
Returning to Zhāowū Shān,
he inspected local customs,
met with elders,
discussed court policies,
and established auspicious and inauspicious rituals.
On the *wùzǐ* day of the twelfth month,
a burnt offering was made at Liánhuā Luò.
In the eighth year, spring, on the *jiǎchén* day of the first month,
Hélǔ was appointed Yílírjǐn of the Diélà Department,
and Hūliè was appointed Tìyǐn.
Télímǐn of the Yúgǔlǐ tribe captured and presented the rebel leaders Bùhú, Yǎlǐzhī, and seventeen others.
The Emperor personally interrogated them.
Their confessions implicated many members of the imperial clan and those who were coerced,
so only the chief culprit Bùhú was flogged to death,
the rest were all pardoned and released.
Huàgē, the son of Yúyuè Shuàilǎn, had repeatedly harbored treacherous plots.
The Emperor always treated him with leniency,
but he repeatedly showed no repentance.
The Emperor summoned elders and ministers to confirm his crimes,
and executed him and his sons,
distributing their wealth to the guards.
Over three hundred rebels interrogated by the authorities
had their cases completed.
The Emperor, considering human life to be of utmost importance,
and that death is irreversible,
granted them a feast for one day,
allowing them to engage in their preferred activities,
according to their lifelong tastes.
As the wine flowed,
some sang, some danced, some played target practice, or wrestled,
each indulging their desires to the fullest.
The next day,
they were sentenced according to the severity of their crimes.
The chief culprit Lágé,
and then Diélàgē,
were still treated by the Emperor as his younger brothers;
he could not bear to put them to death,
so he flogged and released them.
As Yīndǐshí and Ānduān were inherently weak,
and were used by Lágé,
their crimes were all pardoned.
However, Xièlǐ, the son of the former Yúyuè Hèdǐlǐ, and Xiálà, Lágé's wife, had genuinely participated in the rebellion,
so an order was given to hang them both.
Nièlǐ, Yīndǐshí's wife, was coerced,
and Zhānmùgū, Ānduān's wife, had once offered loyal advice,
so both were spared.
Then he said to his attendants:
"Though my younger brothers are clever and shrewd,
they harbor treachery and are deeply evil.
They often boast of their extraordinary wisdom,
but are cruelly ruthless;
gullies can be filled, but their greed is insatiable.
When seeking others' faults,
even a small and pardonable one
is considered as heavy as Mount Tài;
when they themselves commit injustice,
even if it's a great evil,
they consider it lighter than a swan's feather.
They consort with petty individuals,
consult women in their plots,
and collude in evil,
thereby endangering the imperial destiny.
Even if they wish not to fail,
how can they succeed?
Yúlúdúgū, the wife of the Northern Prime Minister Shílǔ, was a close relative to the state.
One day she betrayed me
and followed the rebels.
She died of illness before she could be brought to justice.
This was a punishment from Heaven.
Xièlǐ, since childhood, always ate and slept with me.
The affection and favor shown to him surpassed all other relatives,
yet he and his father turned their backs on great kindness and followed the unrighteous.
How can this be forgiven!"
In the seventh month, autumn, on the *bǐngshēn* day, the first day of the month,
the authorities presented the crimes of over three hundred tribal leaders and their co-conspirators in the rebellion,
and they were all executed in the marketplace.
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"To put people to death,
how could this be my desire?
If they had merely wronged me personally,
I could still have pardoned them.
But these people acted wantonly and without principle,
harming loyal and good people,
inflicting suffering on the populace,
and plundering property.
Previously, the common people had tens of thousands of horses,
but now they all walk.
This has never happened since the founding of the state.
It is truly out of necessity that I execute them."
In the tenth month, winter, on the *jiǎzǐ* day, the first day of the month,
the Kāihuáng Diàn was built on the foundation of the Míngwáng Lóu.
In the ninth year, spring, in the first month,
the Wūgǔ tribe rebelled
and was suppressed.
In the sixth month, summer,
Qí Xíngběn, a military officer from Yōuzhōu, led his clan and three thousand men and women from his subordinates to surrender.
An imperial edict appointed him Jiǎnxiào Shàngshū, Zuǒ Púyè,
granted him the name Wūyù,
and provided him with provisions.
After several days, he departed,
and Zhōu Déwēi, the governor of Yōuzhōu, accepted him.
When an imperial edict sought his return,
Déwēi's reply was disrespectful,
so a southern campaign was deliberated.
In the tenth month, winter, on the *wùshēn* day,
fishing was conducted at Yālù Jiāng.
Xīnluó sent envoys to offer local products as tribute.
Gāolí sent envoys to present precious swords.
Qián Liú, King of Wúyuè, sent Téng Yànxiū to offer tribute.
That year,
the divine number of Jūnjī Tàiyī was seen several times,
and an imperial edict ordered its image to be depicted.
In the first year of Shéncè, spring, on the *bǐngxū* day, the first day of the second month,
the Emperor was in Lónghuà Zhōu.
Yēlǜ Hélǔ, Yílírjǐn of the Diéliè Department, and other officials
led all civil and military officers to request the Emperor to accept a venerable title.
After three petitions, he consented.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
ministers and various vassal states built an altar east of the prefecture.
The Emperor was given the venerable title "Dàshèng Dàmíng Tiānhuáng Dì",
and the Empress was given the title "Yìngtiān Dàmíng Dì Huánghòu".
A general amnesty was declared, and the era name was changed to Shéncè.
Initially,
when digging the ground for the altar,
a golden bell was found,
so the place was named Jīnlíng Gāng.
The forest beside the altar was called Cèsheng Lín.
On the *bǐngchén* day of the third month,
Yílírjǐn Hélǔ of the Diéliè Department was appointed Ālúduǒlǐ Yúyuè.
All officials were promoted in rank, and rewards were distributed with differences.
A three-day feast was granted.
His son Bèi was established as the Crown Prince.
In the fourth month, summer, on the *yǐyǒu* day, the first day of the month,
Lú Guóyòng, Jìn's Jìedùshǐ of Yōuzhōu, surrendered
and was appointed Liúhòu of the Yōuzhōu army and cavalry.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
Liáng sent Láng Gōngyuǎn to congratulate.
On the *gēngyín* day of the sixth month,
Qián Liú, King of Wúyuè, sent Téng Yànxiū to offer tribute.
On the *gēngxū* day of the sixth month,
Taishī Zhè Mǔ, for being obsequious,
was beaten twenty times.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
an edict permitted commoners to cultivate wastelands in Yànlè and Mìyún counties,
〔一八〕and exempted them from taxes and corvée for ten years.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Xuānzhèng Diàn Xuéshì Mǎ Déchén died.
An edict posthumously granted him the title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo,
and awarded him 100,000 *qián* [money]
and 100 *shí* [dan] of grain.
On the *yǐhài* day,
an edict ordered the release of various animals to poor people in the border regions.
In this month,
Xiūgē and Páiyà defeated Sòng troops in Tàizhōu.
〔一九〕
In autumn, on the *yǐyǒu* day of the seventh month,
the emperor held court in the Hánliáng Diàn.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Zhongchéng Yēlǜ Hémài Gē was appointed acting Yílíbì,
and Héngzhàng Lángjūn Yēlǜ Yánshòu was made Yùshǐ Dàfū.
On the *guǐsì* day,
troops were dispatched for a southern campaign.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
four individuals each from the Dīlíbì, Nièlā, and Wūhuì tribes were added to the household of Nánběi Lù Fūrén Pólǐdé,
〔二０〕and seals and ribbons were granted.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
the officers and soldiers of the southern campaign were rewarded.
On this day,
the emperor and the empress dowager paid respects at Jǐngzōng Huángdì’s temple.
On the *gēngwǔ* day of the eighth month,
Gāo Zhèng and one other *jìnshì* were passed.
In winter, in the tenth month,
the use of nets and traps to catch rabbits was prohibited.
On the *jiǎshēn* day of the eleventh month,
Yútián's Zhāng Wénbǎo presented books on inner alchemy.
On the *jiǎyín* day of the twelfth month,
fishing took place at Shěnzǐ Luò.
On the *guǐhài* day,
hunting took place at Hǎocǎo Lǐng.

Lǐ Liàngzuò (李諒祚) of Xià (夏) Kingdom sent an envoy to present a memorial of surrender.
On the day *jiǎwǔ*,
Gāo Jiānú (高家奴), Nánmiàn Línyá (南面林牙), and others were dispatched with an imperial edict to appease and instruct him.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the first day, *bǐngshēn*,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the eleventh month, on the day *xīnmǎo*,
an imperial edict ordered that records be kept of all officials who received transfer according to ritual or were dismissed due to offenses,
and these records were to be reported to the Shūmìyuàn (樞密院) annually.
In the twelfth month, on the first day, *bǐngshēn*,
an imperial edict stipulated that the Fùshǐ (副使) of the Huíhú (回鶻) department should be filled by a Qìdān (契丹) person.
On the day *gēngzǐ*,
in celebration of the Emperor's birthday,
a partial amnesty was granted for crimes of corvée labor and below.
On the day *rénzǐ*,
the Emperor instructed his ministers, saying:
“I and the Sòng (宋) ruler are sworn brothers,
and our good relations have lasted for many years.
I wish to see his painted portrait,
so you may convey this to his envoy.”
In the twenty-third year, in spring, in the first month, on the day *jǐsì*,
the Emperor went to Húntóng Jiāng (混同江).
On the day *guǐyǒu*,
the Emperor hunted at Shuāngzǐ Diàn (雙子淀).
On the day *wùzǐ*,
Xià (夏) Kingdom sent an envoy to offer local products as tribute.
On the day *rénchén*,
the Emperor went to the spring hunting ground.
On the day *jiǎwǔ*,
the Emperor hunted at Pánzhípō (盤直坡).
In the third month, on the day *dīnghài*,
the Emperor visited the tent of the Imperial Younger Brother Chóngyuán (重元).
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day *guǐmǎo*,
Gāolí (高麗) sent an envoy to offer tribute.
On the day *guǐchǒu*,
the Emperor hunted at Hézhǐhūlǐ (合只忽里).
In the fifth month, on the day *jǐsì*,
Lǐ Liàngzuò (李諒祚) requested to present horses and camels,
and an imperial edict allowed him to offer them as annual tribute.
On the day *gēngyín*,
the imperial retinue halted at Yǒng'ān Shān (永安山).
On the day *rénchén*,
Xià (夏) Kingdom sent an envoy to offer tribute.
In the sixth month, on the day *bǐngshēn*,
the Emperor went to Qìng Zhōu (慶州).
On the day *jǐhài*,
the Qìng Líng (慶陵) was visited.
On the day *rényín*,
Wáng Huī (王徽) of Gāolí (高麗) requested official titles for his sons,
and an imperial edict granted them the additional title of Jiǎnxiào Tàiwèi (檢校太尉).
On the day *xīnhài*,
Tǔbō (吐蕃) sent an envoy to offer tribute.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day *jǐsì*,
Lǐ Liàngzuò (李諒祚) of Xià (夏) Kingdom sent an envoy to seek a marriage alliance.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
the Emperor went to the autumn hunting ground.
On the day *jǐmǎo*,
an imperial edict ordered the eight branches of the imperial clan to wear khăn xắc (巾幘).
In the ninth month, on the day *gēngyín*,
the Emperor hunted,
encountered three tigers,
and released dogs to catch them.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day *dīngyǒu*,
the imperial retinue halted at Zhōngjīng (中京).
On the day *wùxū*,
the Emperor visited the newly built Mìshūjiān (祕書監).
On the day *xīnchǒu*,
rites were performed at the ancestral temple.
On the day *guǐchǒu*,
because the Kāitàisì (開泰寺) cast a silver Buddha statue,
a partial amnesty was granted to prisoners in the capital.
On the day *bǐngchén*,
Lǐ Liàngzuò (李諒祚) sent an envoy to present a memorial of oath.
In the eleventh month, on the day *yǐchǒu*,
a chief of Zǔbù (阻卜) offered tribute.
On the day *rénshēn*,

the Emperor, leading his officials, conferred the honorific title Réncí Shèngshàn Qīnxiào Guǎngdé Ānjìng Zhēnchún Yìhé Kuānhòu Chóngjué Yítiān Huángtàihòu (仁慈聖善欽孝廣德安靜貞純懿和寬厚崇覺儀天皇太后) upon the Empress Dowager,
and a general amnesty was declared.
Officials inside and outside the court were promoted with varying grades.
On the day *guǐwèi*,
prisoners were reviewed.
On the day *jiǎshēn*,
all officials conferred the honorific title Qīntiān Fèngdào Yòushì Xīnglì Wǔdìng Wénchéng Shèngshén Rénxiào Huángdì (欽天奉道祐世興曆武定文成聖神仁孝皇帝) upon the Emperor,
and Empress Xiāo (蕭) was formally titled Zhēnyì Cíhé Wénhuì Xiàojìng Guǎng'ài Chóngshèng Huánghòu (貞懿慈和文惠孝敬廣愛崇聖皇后).
In the twelfth month, on the day *bǐngshēn*,
the Emperor went to Zhōnghuì Chuān (中會川).
In the twenty-fourth year, in spring, in the first month, on the day *guǐhài*,
the Emperor went to Húntóng Jiāng (混同江).
On the day *wùchén*,
the Empress Dowager was paid respects.
On the day *xīnsì*,
Sòng (宋) sent an envoy to offer congratulations,
and presented trained elephants.
In the second month, on the first day, *jǐchǒu*,
the Sòng (宋) envoy was summoned to fish and compose poetry.
On the day *guǐsì*,
the Emperor went to Chángchūn Hé (長春河).
On the day *jiǎyín*,
Xià (夏) Kingdom sent an envoy to offer congratulations.
In the third month, on the day *guǐhài*,
the Imperial Younger Brother Chóngyuán (重元) had a son,
and a partial amnesty was granted for crimes of corvée labor and below in the temporary imperial residence and in Chángchūn (長春) and Zhènběi (鎮北) prefectures.
In summer, in the fifth month,
the imperial retinue halted at Nányá (南崖).
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day *rényǐn*,
the Emperor went to the autumn hunting ground.
Upon reaching the northern valley of Nányá (南崖),
he became unwell.
In the eighth month, on the day *dīnghài*,
his illness worsened considerably.
Hóngjī (洪基), Yānzhào Guówáng (燕趙國王), was summoned,
and instructed on the essentials of governing the country.
On the day *wùzǐ*,
a general amnesty was declared,
the falcons and eagles of the five falconries were released,
and fishing equipment was burned.
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
the Emperor passed away at the imperial temporary palace,
at the age of forty.
His dying edict named Yānzhào Guówáng (燕趙國王) Hóngjī (洪基) as his successor.
In the first year of Qīngníng (清寧), in the tenth month, on the day *gēngzǐ*,
the honorific posthumous title Shénshèng Xiàozhāng Huángdì (神聖孝章皇帝) was conferred,
and the temple name was Xīngzōng (興宗).
In the fourth year, spring, first month, on the *rénzǐ* day,
went to Yú'érluò.
On the *jǐsì* day,
moved the poor people of Zǔbǔ and others to Shānqián.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
the Sòng dispatched an envoy to present brocade and silk.
Third month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
visited Chūnzhōu.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
the officials in charge reported that the Yellow River had cleared.
Summer, fourth month, on the *xīnchǒu* day,
due to rain,
hunting was suspended.
Fifth month, on the *guǐyǒu* day,
Nàyě reported a victory on the northern frontier.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
stayed at Sālǐnǎi.
Sixth month, on the *wùyín* day (the first day of the month),
the Xià kingdom was attacked by Sòng,
and sent an envoy to request aid.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Nèilǐ, the Jìedùshǐ of Liáoxīngjūn, was appointed Tìyǐn,
and Yēlǜ Guōsān, formerly in charge of Tìyǐn affairs, was appointed Nánjīng Tǒngjūnshǐ.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Niú Wēnshū, a Cānzhīzhèngshì, was additionally appointed in charge of the Liúshǒu of Zhōngjīng.
Autumn, seventh month, on the *wùwǔ* day,
went to Hēilǐng.
Winter, tenth month, on the *yǐhài* day (the first day of the month),
stayed at Ǒusīdànd.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Wòtèlā, the Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng, was additionally appointed Dūbùshǔ of the Qìdān Xínggōng,
to instruct Yānguówáng Yánxǐ.
Eleventh month, on the *yǐsì* day (the first day of the month),
Xiāo Yàoshīnǔ, in charge of Yòuyílíbì affairs, and Yēlǜ Yǎn, a Shūmì Zhíxuéshì, were dispatched as envoys to Sòng,
to subtly suggest peace with Xià.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Xià again dispatched an envoy to request aid.
Twelfth month, on the *rénchén* day,
a regeneration ceremony was performed for Yānguówáng Yánxǐ,
and a general amnesty was granted to prisoners within three hundred *lǐ*.
In the fifth year, spring, first month, on the *yǐsì* day,
went to Yú'érluò.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
an imperial edict ordered Xiàguówáng Lǐ Qiánshùn to attack the Básīmǔ and other tribes.
Summer, fifth month, on the *rénxū* day,
Yàoshīnǔ and others returned from their mission to Sòng,
reporting that Sòng had ceased military action.
On the *guǐhài* day,
visited the Qiánlíng tomb.
On the *wùchén* day,
Wòtèlā, the Nánfǔ Zǎixiàng, was additionally appointed Xīběilù Zhāotǎoshǐ,
and Jīnjūn Dūwěi.
On the *jǐsì* day,
stayed at Yánliǔhú.
Sixth month, on the *jiǎshēn* day,
Huílíbǎo, the Dàwáng of the Xī Lìubù, was appointed Qìdān Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ,
and Xiāo Yàoshīnǔ, in charge of Yòuyílíbì affairs, was appointed Nánmiàn Línyá,
and additionally in charge of Qìdān Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ affairs.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the tribal chiefs of Wǔguó came to court.
On the *wùxū* day,
Zǔbǔ came to pay tribute.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Yēlǜ Hǎojiānú, the Xīngshènggōngshǐ, was appointed Yòuyílíbì.
Autumn, seventh month, on the *rénzǐ* day (the first day of the month),
Tìdécháng Tūdī and others came to pay tribute.
On the *xīnhài* day,
went to Dàláogǔshān.
Intercalary ninth month, on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
stayed at Dúlújīn.
Winter, tenth month, on the *jǐhài* day (the first day of the month),
Gāolíwáng Yóng dispatched an envoy to request investiture.
On the *dīngsì* day,
Wòtèlā reported a victory in the campaign against Yēdúguā.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Xiāo Délǐdǐ, the Tóngzhī Nánjīngliúshǒushì, was appointed Zhī Běiyuàn Shūmìshǐshì.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Sòng dispatched Guō Zhīzhāng and Cáo Píng to convey good wishes.
On the *wùchén* day,
relief was provided to the famine-stricken in Liáozhōu,
and their rent and taxes were remitted for one year.
Eleventh month, on the *jiǎxū* day,
relief was provided to the Nán and Běi Èrjiū.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Xià kingdom, because Sòng had ceased military action,
dispatched an envoy to express gratitude.
Twelfth month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
Zhào Xiàoyán, a Cānzhīzhèngshì, was appointed Hànrén Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ,
and Liáng Yuán, the Hànrén Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ, was appointed Liáoxīngjūn Jìedùshǐ.
In the sixth year, spring, first month, on the *guǐyǒu* day,
Yēlǜ Wúyě, the Nányuàn Dàwáng, passed away.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Tūkāiqǐ, a Tàishī who had retired from office, was appointed Xī Lìubù Dàwáng.
On the *dīnghài* day,
went to Chūnshuǐ.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Wòtèlā captured Mógǔsī and presented him.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
an imperial edict inquired about the people's hardships.
Second month, on the *dīngwèi* day,
Chénjiānú, the Wūgǔbù Jìedùshǐ, was appointed Nányuàn Dàwáng.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
Mógǔsī was executed by dismemberment in the marketplace.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
silk was distributed to the poor people of Wǔyuàn.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Sòng dispatched an envoy to announce that Sòngzhǔ Xù had passed away,
and his younger brother Jí had succeeded to the throne;
on the same day, an envoy was dispatched to offer condolences.
Third month, on the *jiǎshēn* day,
the prohibitions on mountains and forests in Shuòzhōu were relaxed.
Summer, fourth month, on the *dīngyǒu* day (the first day of the month),
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
went to Tànshān.
Fifth month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
the Wūgǔbù attacked Cházhálà,
and defeated them.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Zhào Xiàoyán, the Hànrén Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ, passed away.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
stayed at Nàgáluò.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Sòng dispatched an envoy to present relics of the late Emperor.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Hé Lǔsǎogǔ, the Dōngjīng Liúshǒu, was appointed Tìyǐn,
and Xiāo Chánggē, the Nányuàn Xuānhuīshǐ, was appointed Hànrén Xínggōng Dūbùshǔ.
Sixth month, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
an envoy was dispatched to congratulate the Sòngzhǔ.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
because the official documents of the authorities recorded the Sòng Emperor's
"succeeding to the throne"
as
"ascending the precious throne,"
an imperial edict stripped Zǎixiàng Zhèng Zhuān and others below him of their offices,
and dismissed Zhuān to be in charge of Xīngzhōngfǔ affairs,
Hán Zīràng to be Jìedùshǐ of Chóngyìjūn,
and Yùshǐzhōngchéng Hán Jūnyì to be Jìedùshǐ of Guǎngshùnjūn.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
the Zǔbǔ chieftain came to pay tribute.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
an envoy was dispatched to resolve outstanding prison cases in the Wǔjīng.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
Liáng Yuán, the Liáoxīngjūn Jìedùshǐ, was appointed Shūmì Fùshǐ.
Autumn, seventh month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
went to Shālǐng.
On the *rénshēn* day,
the Yēdúguā tribes raided the Xīběilù.
Eighth month,
Wòtèlā attacked and defeated them with troops,
and sent an envoy to present the victory report.
Ninth month, on the *guǐwèi* day,
observed a sacrifice at Mùyèshān.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
stayed at Ǒusīdànd.
Winter, tenth month, on the *rénzhōng* day,
Wáng Shīrú, a Shūmì Fùshǐ, was appointed supervisor of the compilation of national history.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
the tribal chiefs of Wǔguó came to pay tribute.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
because Píngzhōu was suffering from famine,
their rent and taxes were remitted for one year.
Eleventh month, on the *rénshēn* day,
as Tiāndéjūn citizen Tián Shìróng lived with three generations under one roof,
an imperial edict granted him an official post,
and ordered one of his sons to serve as Zhīhòu in the Sānbānyuàn.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Zhìdá, a monk from Yīwūlǘshān, was summoned to establish an altar in the inner palace.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Xiàguówáng Lǐ Qiánshùn dispatched an envoy to request marriage to a princess.
Twelfth month, on the *yǐwèi* day,
the Nǚzhēn dispatched an envoy to pay tribute.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Hǎojiānú, in charge of Yòuyílíbì affairs, was appointed Běimiàn Línyá.
On the *xīnhài* day,
an imperial edict ordered Yānguówáng Yánxǐ to nominate officials down to the rank of Dàjiāngjūn.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Tiělí came to pay tribute.
Sòng dispatched an envoy to express gratitude.
The Emperor was unwell.
In this year,
Gāolíwáng Yóng's eldest son, Wǔ, was enfeoffed as Sānguó Gōng.
Eighty-seven *jìnshì* including Kāng Bǐngjiǎn were released.
In the seventh year, spring, first month, on the *rénxū* day (the first day of the month),
despite his illness, the Emperor held court in Qīngfēngdiàn to receive felicitations from officials and envoys from various states.
That night,
a white vapor like a silk ribbon
descended from the sky.
Black clouds rose from the northwest,
flying swiftly and with sound.
In the north, there were blue, red, black, and white vapors,
intermingling and falling.
On the *guǐhài* day,
went to Húntóngjiāng.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Emperor passed away at the traveling palace,
aged seventy.
The last will decreed Yānguówáng Yánxǐ to succeed to the throne.
In the first year of Bǎo Dà (1128), spring, first month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
the reign title was changed,
and a general amnesty was declared.
Originally,
when the Jīn people raised an army,
nearly half of the commanderies and counties were lost.
The Emperor had four sons: the eldest, Zhào Wáng,
whose mother was Zhào Zhāoróng;
the second, Jìn Wáng,
whose mother was Wén Fēi;
the third and fourth, Qín Wáng and Xǔ Wáng,
both born of Yuán Fēi.
The people of the country knew of Jìn Wáng's virtue
and deeply placed their hopes in him.
Yuán Fēi's elder brother, the Grand Counselor Xiāo Fèngxiān, fearing that Qín Wáng would not be established as heir,
secretly plotted.
Wén Fēi had two sisters: the eldest married Yēlǜ Táhélǐ,
the second was Wén Fēi,
and the third married Yú Dǔ.
One day,
when both her elder and younger sisters were assembled at the army front,
Fèngxiān instigated someone to falsely accuse the Imperial son-in-law Xiāo Yù and Yú Dǔ of plotting to establish Jìn Wáng.
When the matter came to light,
Yù, Táhélǐ, and others were executed;
Wén Fēi was also granted death.
Only Jìn Wáng was spared immediate punishment, as the Emperor was reluctant to condemn him.
Yú Dǔ, who was in the army,
was greatly alarmed when he heard of this,
and immediately led over a thousand cavalry to rebel and defect to Jīn.

The Emperor dispatched Xiāo Xiámǎi, who was in charge of the affairs of the Xī King's mansion, the Northern Administration Chancellor Xiāo Dégōng, the Grand Registrar of the Grand Court Yēlǜ Dìlǐgū, the Guī Prefecture Inspector Xiāo Héshàngnú, and the Four Armies Grand Tutor Xiāo Gàn, to lead their respective troops in pursuit.
They caught up with them at Zhūlǘ Shān Xiàn.
The generals deliberated, saying:
"Our Lord believes Xiāo Fèngxiān's words,
and Fèngxiān treats us as nothing.
Yú Dǔ is a valiant and outstanding member of the imperial clan;
he is unwilling to be subservient to Fèngxiān.
If we capture Yú Dǔ,
then one day, all of us will become Yú Dǔ!
It would be better to let him go."
Upon their return,
they fabricated a report, saying:
"We pursued but could not catch up."
Once Fèngxiān saw Yú Dǔ's flight,
he feared that other commanders would also rebel in the future,
so he advised a sudden increase in titles and rewards
to win the hearts of the multitude.
Xiāo Xiámǎi was made Xī Wáng;
Xiāo Dégōng was appointed Acting Grand Councilor of the Central Secretariat and concurrently Administrator of Shàngjīng Prefecture;
Yēlǜ Dìlǐgū was made Commander-in-chief of the Dragon and Tiger Guard;
Xiāo Héshàngnú, Commander-in-chief of the Golden Armor Guard;
and Xiāo Gàn, Grand General Who Guards the State.
In the second month,
the Emperor visited Yuānyāng Luò.
In summer, fifth month,
he reached Hélǐjuè.
In autumn, seventh month,
he hunted at Tàn Shān.
In ninth month,
he reached Nánjīng.
In winter, eleventh month, on the *guǐhài* day,
Zhào Wáng Xíníliè, the Administrator of Xījīng, was made Tìyǐn.
In the second year (1129), spring, first month, on the *yǐhài* day,
Jīn conquered Zhōngjīng
and then captured Zézhōu.
The Emperor exited Jūyōng Guān
and arrived at Yuānyāng Luò.
Upon hearing that Yú Dǔ was leading the Jīn people Lóushì Bólǐn to arrive unexpectedly,
Xiāo Fèngxiān said:
"Yú Dǔ is a descendant of Wángzǐ Bān.
He comes now only to establish his nephew, Jìn Wáng.
If we consider the welfare of the state,
and do not begrudge one son,
clearly accuse and execute him,
then Yú Dǔ will turn back without a battle."
The Emperor then granted Jìn Wáng death.
He wore plain mourning clothes for three days.
Yēlǜ Sābā and others were all executed.
The Prince had always enjoyed popular support,
and when the armies heard of his death,
there was no one who did not shed tears;
consequently, morale disintegrated.
Yú Dǔ led the Jīn people to press upon the traveling palace.
The Emperor led five thousand cavalry of his guard to Yúnzhōng,
abandoning the Imperial Seal of State at the Sānggān Hé.
Second month, on the *gēngyín* day, the first day of the lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Yēlǜ Mǎgē, who was in charge of the affairs of the Northern Division Great King, and Xiāo Tèmò, the Han Chinese Grand Commissioner of the Traveling Palace, were both appointed Grand Commanders;
Yēlǜ Bǔdé, the Superintendent of Tàihé Palace, served as their deputy.
They led troops to garrison at Yuānyāng Luò.
On the *jǐhài* day,
the Jīn army defeated Xī Wáng Xiámò at Běi'ān Zhōu,
and then captured the city.
Third month, on the *xīnyǒu* day,
the Emperor, hearing that the Jīn army was about to emerge from west of the mountains,
then rushed to Báishuǐ Luò.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Mólǔwò, the Superintendent of Herds, surrendered to Jīn.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
the Emperor arrived at Nǚgǔdǐ Cāng.
Hearing that the Jīn army was approaching,
and not knowing what to do,
he rode lightly into Jiā Shān.
Only then did he realize Fèngxiān's disloyalty.
He angrily said:
"Your father and son have led me to this pass;
now I wish to execute you,
but what good would it do for the situation!
I fear the army's resentment,
and if you evade the enemy and seek temporary safety,
disaster will surely befall me.
Do not follow me."
Fèngxiān dismounted,
cried, bowed, and departed.
Before he had traveled a few *lǐ*,
his attendants seized his father and son,
bound them, and sent them to the Jīn army.
The Jīn people beheaded his eldest son, Áng,
and sent Fèngxiān and his second son, Yù, in chains to the Jīn ruler.
On the way, they met Liáo troops,
who seized them and returned them to their country,

Originally,

Chǔwēn, hearing that the Emperor had entered Jiā Shān,
and that communication of orders had been cut off for several days,
immediately conspired with his younger brother Chǔnéng and his son Shì,
outwardly feigning to join the rebellious troops,
and inwardly forming a pact with the Grand Commander Xiāo Gàn,
to enthrone Chún.

Consequently, he, along with other high officials Yēlǜ Dàshí, Zuǒ Qǐgōng, Yú Zhòngwén, Cáo Yǒngyì, Kāng Gōngbì, assembled tens of thousands of Qīdān and Han officials, various army units, and elders at Chún's residence.
Chǔwēn invited Zhāng Lín to attend
and explained the matter to him.
Lín said:
"Acting as regent would be acceptable."
Chǔwēn replied:
"Heaven's will and the people's hearts are already decided;
please establish him."
Chǔwēn and others asked Chún to receive the ceremony.
As Chún came out,
Lǐ Shì held a crimson robe and draped it over him,
ordering the officials to bow, dance, and shout "Long live!"
Chún was shocked and alarmed,
and repeatedly declined,
but was compelled to comply.
Chǔwēn was appointed Grand Commandant;

were all granted the *jìnshì* degree,

the Imperial Son-in-law Commandant Xiāo Dàn, Commissioner of Military Affairs.
The 'Rebellious Army' was renamed the 'Ever Victorious Army'.
Thereupon, a general amnesty was declared,

What Tiānzuò still possessed

Tàizǔ ascended the throne for five years,
campaigning against the Western Xī and Eastern Xī.
He pacified them all,
and gained control of all the people of Xī and Xī.
In the spring of the sixth year,
he personally led an expedition to Yōuzhōu.
The banners of the east and west were visible to each other,
stretching for hundreds of lǐ.
The prefectures and counties he passed through
all submitted at the mere sight of his army.
He captured a great many,
then returned with his victorious army.
In the autumn,
he personally led an expedition against the Bèiyīn Guó,
capturing tens of thousands.
In the first year of Shéncè,
he personally led an expedition against the various tribes of Tūjué, Tǔhún, Dǎngxiàng, Xiǎofān, and Shātuó,
capturing 15,600 households.
He attacked Zhènwǔ,
and, taking advantage of his victory, marched eastward,
attacking the five prefectures of Wèi, Xīn, Wǔ, Guī, and Rú.
The number of captives was innumerable,
and 14,700 who resisted were beheaded.
He gained control of all the people of Dàiběi, Héqu, and Yīnshān,
and consequently seized the eight armies north of the mountains.
In the fourth year,
he personally led an expedition against the Gǔlǐ Guó,
capturing 14,200 people.
In the fifth year,
he campaigned against Dǎngxiàng,
capturing 2,600 people.
He attacked Tiāndé Jūn,
destroying twelve palisades,
and relocating their people.
In the sixth year,
he exited Jūyōng Guān,
and divided his troops to raid Tán, Shùn, and other prefectures,
as well as Ānyuǎn Jūn, Sānhé, Liángxiāng, Wàngdū, Lù, Mǎnchéng, Suìchéng, and other counties.
He captured their people and relocated them to the interior.
The Crown Prince attacked and pacified Dìngzhōu,
capturing a great many.
In the first year of Tiānzàn,
due to the increasing population
and the looseness of administration,
he divided the great Wūgǔ from the north into two parts,
establishing two military governors to govern them.
In the third year,
he led a western expedition against Dǎngxiàng and other states,
capturing innumerable people.
In the fourth year,
he again personally led an expedition against Bóhǎi.
In the first year of Tiānxiǎn,
he destroyed the Bóhǎi Guó,
which had a territory of five thousand lǐ,
an army of several hundred thousand,
five capitals, fifteen prefectures, and sixty-two districts.
He gained control of all its people,
and the Qìdān thereby grew larger.
At the beginning of Huìtóng,
Tàizōng destroyed Táng and established Jìn.
Jìn offered the sixteen prefectures of Yān and Dài.
With a numerous populace and strong army,
no one could resist them.
Military System
Regarding the military system of Liáo Guó,
all commoners aged fifteen and above,
and below fifty,
were registered in the military.
For each principal soldier,
there were three horses,
and one household attendant each for foraging, guarding the camp, and performing odd jobs.
Each person had nine items of iron armor,
horse saddles and bridles,
and horse armor made of leather and iron,
depending on their strength.
Four bows,
four hundred arrows,

one long and short spear, one *gē* (dagger-axe), one axe-halberd, one small banner, one hammer-awl, one fire-striker and flint, one horse trough, one *bǐng* (ration) of one dòu, one *xiá* (pouch), and one collapsible umbrella.
Two hundred chǐ of horse tethering rope
were all self-provided.
Neither men nor horses were supplied with rations or fodder.
Foraging cavalry were dispatched daily in all four directions to plunder and supply them.
Gold fish tallies were cast
to mobilize military horses.
There were two hundred silver plaques for capturing horses and transmitting orders.
At the army's encampment,
there were distant reconnaissance scouts on horseback
who listened for the sound of people and horses at night.
Whenever troops were raised,
the Emperor, accompanied by both civilian and military officials of the Fān and Hàn,
sacrificed a black ox and a white horse to heaven and earth and the sun god.
They did not bow to the moon.
He then commanded close officials to report to the tombs of Tàizǔ and his successors, as well as the Mùyè Shān deity,
and then issued edicts to various circuits to conscript soldiers.
Only the kings of Nán and Běi Xī,
the Bóhǎi troops of Dōngjīng,
and the統軍 troops of Yānjīng,
even upon receiving the edict,
would not dare to dispatch troops
without first reporting it.
The Emperor would send a great general carrying a gold fish tally,
and only when they matched
would the troops set out.
Upon first hearing the edict,
households and their able-bodied men were assembled.
Their household resources were assessed,
and registers were verified and people gathered to await orders.
From the ten-man commander and above,
they successively mustered and gathered military horses and weaponry.
When the tally arrived,
the military horses were led by their respective bureaus;
the envoy was not allowed to interfere.
Only after jointly reviewing the military horses
was another report made to the Emperor.
Based on the number of military horses,
an envoy was again appointed as the army commander,
who would supervise the respective bureaus.
They then requested to display the flags and drums of the five directions,
before the Emperor personally reviewed the generals and officers.
Furthermore, distinguished relatives and high-ranking ministers were selected
to serve as commander-in-chief, deputy commander-in-chief, and inspector-general of the field army, one of each.
In addition, thirty thousand of the most elite soldiers from various armies were selected as the imperial guard.
Three thousand brave and strong men were selected as the vanguard.
More than one hundred fierce and strong men were selected as distant reconnaissance scouts.
All of the above had their own commanders.
Furthermore, in each division of the various armies,
depending on its size,
ten or five men were drawn out
to form a squad,
with a separate commander established
to facilitate the requisition of soldiers and horses
and the transmission of official documents.
For southern expeditions, troop mobilization
often occurred at Yuānyāng Pō, a thousand lǐ north of Yōuzhōu.
When marching,
they generally took routes through Jūyōng Guān, Cáowáng Yù, Báimǎ Kǒu, Gǔběi Kǒu, Āndámǎ Kǒu, Sōngtíng Guān, and Yú Guān.
Upon approaching the borders of Píngzhōu and Yōuzhōu,
envoys were again dispatched to urge them on by separate routes,
not allowing them to stay long,
for fear of trampling crops.
Troops would not be deployed after September,
and would not return after December.
On the road, they were not allowed to see monks, nuns, or people in mourning attire.

The Three Sovereigns and Holy Sages,
in an era of pristine simplicity,
had double gates and clappers,
even stricter than for violent guests.
The ancestors of the Liáo,
before they had the security of cities, moats, and palaces,
used felt carts as camps,
and fortified stockades as palaces,
so the officials of the Imperial Tent had to be cautious.
Those from the imperial clan served as bodyguards;
Zhùzhàng served as close attendants;
Northern and Southern tribes served as guards;
military officials served as residential guards;
the imperial army served as imperial guards;
and all officials taking turns served as night watchmen.
Fèngchén oversaw imperial provisions;
the Three Divisions ensured solemnity at court assemblies;
and the fortified stockades maintained strictness day and night.
The legal system could be described as strict and meticulous.

In ancient times, criminals were not kept by the ruler's side.
The families of rebels were confiscated and made into Zhùzhàng,
serving as imperial guards,
which could make one tremble with fear.
This is perhaps why the Liáo dynasty saw so many disturbances erupt from within.

Shìzōng completely pardoned them.

Auspicious Rites
Mountain Worship Ceremony: The positions of the heavenly deities (Tiānshén) and earthly spirits (Dìzhī) are set up on Mùyèshān,
facing east.
A sovereign tree (jūnshù) is erected in the center,
with a cluster of trees planted in front,
to symbolize the court assembly.
Additionally, two trees are planted in pairs,
to serve as the spirit gate (shénmén).
When the emperor (Huángdì) and empress (Huánghòu) arrive,
the Yílíbì (夷離畢) prepares the ritual.
The sacrificial animals are a reddish-white horse, a black ox, and a reddish-white sheep,
all male.
The servant official, called Qígǔ Zhuàilá (旗鼓拽剌),
slaughters the animals,
carves the bodies,
and hangs them on the sovereign tree.
The Grand Shaman (Tàiwū) libates the animals with wine.
The ritual official, called Dílièmádū (敵烈麻都),
announces,
"The ceremony is complete."
The emperor wears a golden crown with golden patterns,
a white damask robe,
a crimson belt,
a hanging fish ornament,
three crimson tassels hanging from a mountain pattern,
decorated with rhinoceros horn and jade knives and whetstones,
and black boots with embroidered seams.
The empress wears a crimson skirt (or similar garment indicated by the ● character),
a red robe with embroidered seams,
a hanging jade pendant,
a double-knotted headscarf,
and black boots with embroidered seams.
The emperor and empress ride on saddled horses.
The officials stand to the south,
and the court ladies (mìngfù) to the north,
wearing the colors of their respective tribal banners.
The emperor and empress dismount in front of the sovereign tree,
ascend the southern altar, and sit on the imperial couch (yùtà).
The officials and court ladies arrange themselves in their respective ranks,
entering in order to take their positions;
they form a combined rank,
bow,
and return to their places.
The emperor and empress proceed to the positions of the heavenly deities (Tiānshén) and earthly spirits (Dìzhī),
and offer libations.
After the Héménshǐ (閤門使) finishes reading the prayer,
they return to their seats.
The Northern Chancellor (Běifǔ Zǎixiàng) and Tìyǐn (惕隱) then offer libations to the sovereign tree,
and then to all the cluster of trees.
Music plays.
The officials and court ladies withdraw.
The emperor, leading the clans of the Mèngfù (孟父), Zhòngfù (仲父), and Jìfù (季父),
circles the spirit gate trees three times.
Other clans circle seven times.
The emperor and empress bow twice,
and all those present also bow twice.
Incense is offered,
and they bow twice as before.
The emperor and empress ascend the altar,
and sit on a square cushion with a dragon pattern (lóngwén fāngyīn).
A warning is sounded twice,
and they proceed to the eastern place of sacrifice.
The officials and court ladies follow,
arranged in ranks as before.
The shaman (wū) wears white robes,
and the Tìyǐn (惕隱) bows and places a plain scarf (sùjīn) on his head.
The shaman delivers three addresses.
With each address,
the emperor and empress bow once,
and all those present also bow once.
The emperor and empress each offer two goblets of wine
and two dishes of meat,
making a second libation.
The ministers and court ladies, holding one dish of wine in their right hand
and one dish of meat in their left,
stand slightly behind,
and make one libation.
The Tìyǐn (惕隱) is instructed to throw them eastward.
The emperor and empress bow six times,
and all those present also bow six times.
The emperor and empress return to their positions,
and sit.
The Cáo Zhōngchéng (中丞) is ordered to present tea and fruit,
and two dishes each of cakes and pastries,
offering them to the positions of the heavenly deities (Tiānshén) and earthly spirits (Dìzhī).
Twenty Zhíshì Lángjūn (執事郎君) carrying auspicious wine (fújǐu) and sacrificial meat (zuòròu)
proceed before the emperor and empress.
After the Grand Shaman (Tàiwū) completes the libation,
the emperor and empress bow twice,
and all those present also bow twice.
The emperor and empress bow once,
drink the auspicious wine,
receive the sacrificial meat,
return to their positions,
and sit.
Those present drink in turn.
The emperor and empress lead the officials back to their ranks,
and bow twice.
A warning is sounded,
and they bow once.
They withdraw.
Tàizōng (太宗) visited the Dàbēigé (大悲閣) in Yōuzhōu (幽州),
moved the statue of the White-Robed Guānyīn (Báiyī Guānyīn),
built a temple on Mùyèshān,
and revered her as a household deity (jiāshén).
After the tree-circling part of the Mountain Worship Ceremony,
a section
"Proceeding to the Bodhisattva Hall Ceremony" (Yì Púsàtáng Yí)
was added,
after which the deities were worshipped.
This was not due to Húlà Kèhán (胡剌可汗).
Xīngzōng (興宗) first conducted ceremonies at the Bodhisattva Hall and for the deities of Mùyèshān
and the Liáohé (遼河),
and then performed the Mountain Worship Ceremony.
The crowns, robes, and ritual procedures were greatly changed,
and later became the norm.
Deities residing in trees,
the display of sacrificed animals announcing completion,
ritual positions for libations and prayers,
and the offering of blessings and drinking of auspicious wine
often coincidentally aligned with proper rites.
The principles of Heaven and human sentiment
are applicable universally
and truly so.
The reforms of Xīngzōng (興zōng),
not being based on canonical scholarship,
could not significantly surpass the past,
and therefore are not recorded.
Sèsè Ceremony: If there is a drought,

Before the day,
a hundred-pillar heavenly canopy (bǎizhù tiānpéng) is erected.
On the day itself,
the emperor offers libations to the imperial portraits of the former emperors (Xiāndì Yùróng),
and then shoots arrows at a willow.
The emperor shoots twice,
and the imperial princes (qīnwáng) and grand councilors (zǎizhí) each shoot once in turn.
Those who hit the willow stake their robes and hats,
while those who miss stake their robes and hats.
The loser offers a drink to the winner,
and then each reclaims their robes and hats.
The next day,
a willow is planted southeast of the heavenly canopy.
Shamans (wū) offer wine,
millet, and coarse grain to the planted willow,
and pray to it.
After the emperor and empress finish sacrificing to the east,
their children shoot arrows at the willow.
Imperial clan members (huángzú), maternal uncles of the emperor (guójìu), officials, and participants in the ceremony
are given gifts according to their rank.
If it rains for three days,
the Dílièmádū (敵烈麻都) is granted four horses and four sets of clothing;
otherwise, he is doused with water.
In the first year of Qīngníng (清寧) of Dàozōng (道宗),
after the emperor finished shooting the willow,
he proceeded to the Altar of the Wind Master (Fēngshī Tán),
and bowed twice.
Song envoys’ funeral sacrifice, condolence, and comfort ceremony: The Grand Empress Dowager proceeded to the Cuōtú Diàn,
wearing mourning attire.
The Empress Dowager sat on the north side, facing south, with a curtain drawn.
The Emperor sat on the south side, facing north.
The Song envoys arrived at their temporary lodging.
They were granted plain clothes and black sashes.
After changing,
the northern and southern officials were led in to take their places
and stand still.
Those allowed to sit on low stools or below
all ascended the殿 (diàn) and stood in their positions.
First, the sacrificial envoy and deputy, holding the sacrificial text, entered through the south cave gate.
All officials above and below the殿 (diàn) raised a wail of sorrow,
and stood still at the Dānchí.
The Xīshàng Gémén Shǐ descended from the south steps,
received the sacrificial text,
ascended the殿 (diàn) to open the seal,
placed it on the incense table,
and the wailing ceased.
The sacrificial offerings were arranged in front of the殿 (diàn).
The envoy and deputy were led up the south steps to the殿 (diàn),
stood at the cushioned mat,
bowed,
and bowed twice again.
The Grand Envoy was led forward to offer incense,
then retreated,
and bowed twice again.
The Grand Envoy knelt forward,
held the ceremonial cup,
and offered three libations of wine.
The Jiàofāng played music.
He retreated,
and bowed twice again.
The two Zhōngshū Shèrén were beckoned to kneel and hold the sacrificial text.
The Grand Envoy was led forward to prostrate himself and kneel.
After the reading was finished,
a wail of sorrow was raised.
The envoy and deputy were led down the殿 (diàn) to stand still,
and the wailing ceased.
After the offering beds were all brought out,
the envoy and deputy were led to the south side,
facing north, to stand.
The condolence envoy and deputy were summoned to enter through the south cave gate.
The four envoys together saw the spirit of the late Emperor Dàxíng,
and bowed twice.
They were led out
to return to their temporary lodging.
The Empress Dowager sat in a separate殿 (diàn),
wearing mourning attire.
First, the northern and southern officials were led to stand in their places above and below the殿 (diàn).
The condolence envoy and deputy, holding the letter box, entered from the right,
and stood in the middle of the殿 (diàn).
The Gémén Shǐ descended from the right side of the殿 (diàn) to receive the letter box,
ascended the殿 (diàn) and reported,
“The seal is intact.”
After it was opened and read,
the envoy and deputy were led up the south steps to the殿 (diàn).
After conveying the condolences,
they retreated,
and descended the殿 (diàn) to stand.
After the offering beds were all brought past,
the envoy and deputy were led to the south side,
facing north, to stand.
The sacrificial envoy and deputy were summoned to enter.
The four envoys together presented themselves,
bowed,
and bowed twice again.
Without leaving their ranks,
they reported,
“May Your Majesty be blessed with ten thousand fortunes,”
and bowed twice again.
They left their ranks,
expressed gratitude for seeing the Emperor’s countenance,
and bowed twice again,
then stood still.
The Xuān Huī conveyed the imperial decree of comfort and inquiry.
They expressed gratitude in their positions,
and bowed twice again.
They were led out
to return to their temporary lodging.
The Emperor resided in the Nándiàn,
wearing mourning attire.
The envoy and deputy entered to have an audience,
following the ceremony for seeing the Empress Dowager,
with added expressions of gratitude for the distant reception, comfort, and medicines,
and bowed twice again.
Next, gifts were bestowed upon the envoy, deputy, and accompanying personnel.
The sacrificial envoy and deputy were separately granted customary items for reading the sacrificial text.
A banquet was hosted at the official residence on the same day.
The ceremonies for envoys from Gāolí and Xiàguó offering condolences and contributions
were generally similar.
When Dàozōng passed away,
Emperor Tiānzuò inquired about the rites from Yēlǜ Gù.
The State of Sòng dispatched envoys to offer condolences, present sacrifices, and return funerary gifts.
The Emperor wore mourning attire
and resided in a separate殿 (diàn) north of the Yóuxiān.
When the envoys entered the gate,
the Emperor wept.
The envoys proceeded to the coffin to offer incense.
After reading the sacrificial text,
they wept again.
The officials read the imperial will,
and wept uncontrollably.
The envoys exited.
A short while later,
they re-entered
and arranged the funerary gifts in front of the coffin.
The Emperor came to supervise and weep.
He retreated,
changed clothes,
and resided in the tent殿 (diàn) south of the Yóuxiān Diàn.
The envoys entered for an audience and to take their leave.
An imperial edict commanded officials to host a banquet at the official residence.
Song envoys’ announcement of sorrow ceremony: The Emperor wore plain cap and attire,
and the officials wore black robes and black sashes.
The Song envoy, holding the letter, entered from the right
and stood within the Dānchí.
The Xīshàng Gémén Shǐ descended from the right steps of the殿 (diàn),
received the letter box,
ascended the殿 (diàn),
bowed within the balustrade,
and reported,
“The seal is intact.”
After it was opened,
it was handed to the Zǎixiàng on a table west of the殿 (diàn) to be read.
The Emperor raised a wail of sorrow.
A Shèrén led the envoy up the right steps.
He prostrated and knelt within the balustrade.
After conveying greetings,
he rose from prostration
and stood.
The Emperor inquired,
“May the Emperor of the Southern Court be blessed with ten thousand fortunes?”
The envoy knelt and reported,
“When I departed, His Majesty was blessed with ten thousand fortunes.”
He rose
and retreated.
A Shèrén led the envoy down the right steps of the殿 (diàn).
West of the Dānchí,
he bowed facing east.
The Tōngshì Shèrén announced the envoy’s name for audience,
and he bowed twice.
Without leaving his ranks,
he reported,
“May Your Majesty be blessed with ten thousand fortunes,”
and bowed twice again.
He left his ranks,
expressed gratitude for seeing the Emperor’s countenance,
and bowed twice again.
He then left his ranks again
and expressed gratitude for the distant reception, comfort, and medicines,
and bowed twice again.
He was prompted to wait,
led out,
and proceeded to his temporary lodging,
where clothes and items were bestowed.
The accompanying personnel were led in.
Their names were announced for bowing,
and they reported,
“May Your Majesty be blessed with ten thousand fortunes.”
They left for their lodging,
where clothes were bestowed,
in a ceremony similar to that of the envoy.
The envoy was then led in again,
bowed facing the殿 (diàn),
and was prompted to express gratitude for the grace.
He was prompted again,
“There is an imperial decree to bestow a banquet,”
and bowed twice.
He was prompted to wait,
and proceeded to his temporary lodging for the banquet.
The accompanying personnel expressed gratitude for the grace
and bowed for the imperial decree bestowing a banquet,
all as before.
After the banquet,
they returned to the official residence.
Protocol for the Song Envoy presenting tribute and gifts: All officials, before dawn, in court attire,
stood in ranks before the palace hall.
The Song tribute envoy and the envoy for announcing the emperor's ascension, with their deputies, entered the inner gate.
The attendant vice-envoy (Guǎnbàn Fùshǐ) led the envoy for announcing the ascension (Xiè Dēngwèi Shǐ) to his tent for seating.
The attendant grand envoy (Guǎnbàn Dàshǐ) and the tribute envoy and his deputy presented a letter and entered,
stopping at the felt mat outside the western upper palace gate (Xīshàng Gémén).
The palace gate official (Géménshǐ) received the letter box,
placing it on a table below the western steps of the hall.
The usher (Yǐnjìnshǐ) led the tribute items through the western upper palace gate,
then out through the side gate in the corridor.
The emperor ascended the hall and took his seat.
The Xuanhuīshǐ (Commissioner of Military Affairs) led the ranks before the hall in paying respects.
Then the prime ministers (Zǎichén) led the civil and military ranks in paying respects.
The Zhōngshūlìng (Chancellor) was led up the western steps to the hall,
to present the Song envoy's memorial (Jiàn Bǎngzi).
The Qìdān officials paid their respects.
The Kònghèguān (Crane Controlling Officials) paid their respects.
The tribute envoy and his deputy entered through the western upper palace gate,
standing facing the hall.
The palace attendant (Shèrén) led the envoy and his deputy up the western steps to the hall,
where they verbally paid their respects.
They were then led down the western steps,
to the east of the vermilion courtyard (Dānchí),
bowed facing west,
announced their names, and reported,
"May the sacred person enjoy ten thousand blessings,"
following the protocol of the envoy for announcing mourning (Gào'āi Shǐ).
They offered thanks for seeing the celestial countenance,
and thanks for the distant reception, the inquiries, and the medicine.
The retinue of the tribute envoy also saw the emperor and followed the same procedure.
Next, the envoy for announcing the emperor's ascension (Gào Dēngwèi Shǐ) and his deputy presented the letter box,
entering through the eastern upper palace gate (Dōngshàng Gémén),
standing facing the hall.
The palace gate official went down the eastern steps,
to receive the letter box.
After the Zhōngshūlìng had read it,
the palace attendant led the envoy and his deputy up the eastern steps to the hall,
to verbally pay their respects.
They were then led down the hall,
standing facing south.
The gifts for announcing the ascension entered,
then exited through the side gate in the corridor.
They withdrew,
bowed facing west,
verbally paid their respects,
and gave thanks for seeing the celestial countenance, the distant reception, etc.,
all following the protocol of the tribute envoy.
Imperial gifts of clothing and other items were bestowed upon the tribute and ascension envoys and their deputies, and their retinues,
as for the envoy for announcing mourning.
All officials who were to be seated ascended the hall and stood in their places.
The two envoys and their deputies were separately led to stand in the two corridors.
The emperor asked the envoys and their deputies,
"Was the journey difficult?"
They prostrated five times within the vermilion courtyard.
Each was led up to the hall to stand in the imperial guard's waiting position.
High ministers presented wine.
The emperor drank wine.
A Qìdān interpreter (Tōng) spoke,
a Han Chinese official (Hànrén Zàn) delivered eulogies.
All officials in the hall bowed,
shouting
"Long live!"
After the eulogies, everyone took their seats.
After the serving of wine, delicacies, tea, meals, and steamed buns,
and after the retinue had finished their watered rice,
all officials rose.
The Qìdān interpreter spoke,
the Han Chinese official delivered eulogies,
all bowed twice,
shouting
"Long live!"
Everyone waited in attendance.
Only the Song envoys and their deputies were led down the hall to offer thanks,
prostrating five times.
They were then led out.
The Kònghèguān waited outside the gate,
reported to the palace gate official that there was no further business,
and the Gòngfèngguān (Officials of the Bureau of Supply) exited in formation.
Protocol for the Gāolì and Xiàguó envoys announcing a ruler's death: A few days in advance,
imperial tents were set up to the left and right of the temporary palace (Xínggōng),
and the envoys' tents were arranged to the southeast.
On the appointed day,
officials from the Northern Department (Běimiàn Chénliáo) wore their everyday attire,
while other officials wore court attire,
and entered for the audience.
When the envoys arrived at their tents,
the relevant authorities (Yǒusī) first presented the memorial of the successor (Sìzǐ Biǎozhuàng) to the Shūmìyuàn (Bureau of Military Affairs),
to be prepared for imperial presentation.
First, officials from the Northern Department and those of "Dwarf Mound" (Ǎiduàn) rank and above were led close to the imperial tent,
standing opposite each other.
Other officials stood according to their ranks and positions.
The envoy announcing the ruler's death (Gàozhōng Rénshǐ) was led in from the right,
reaching the vermilion courtyard,
and stood facing the hall.
He was led up to the right,
stood;
bowed slightly forward,
bowed,
knelt and presented his report.
An imperial inquiry was proclaimed.
If a successor had already been established,
he would humbly receive the imperial decree.
After the report,
he returned to his position.
If a successor had not yet been established,
no imperial inquiry was proclaimed.
He was led down to the vermilion courtyard on the right,
bowing facing north.
After calling out the ranks,
he was led to face the hall and bow twice.
He did not leave his rank,
but reported,
"May the sacred person enjoy ten thousand blessings,"
and bowed twice.
He left his rank,
thanked for seeing the celestial countenance,
returned to his position,
and bowed twice.
He left his rank,
thanked for the distant reception,
returned to his position,
and bowed twice.
After the eulogies, he waited,
then withdrew to his tent.
He re-entered,
as before, bowed facing north,
offered his condolences,
and bowed twice;
longing for the palace,
he bowed twice.
The eulogist said,
"May you have a good journey."
The ceremony concluded.

six sides,

In the second year of Mùzōng's Yìnglì reign,

Presented by the Jìn emperor;

used as a seal knob,

Dàozōng bestowed an eagle-knob seal upon Yēlǜ Rénxiān,

Tallies and Credentials:
Since the time the eight tribes of the Dàhè Shì engaged in warfare,
they would join tallies to mobilize,
which was merely carving wood to form matching halves.
When Tàizǔ received the Mandate,
he replaced them with golden fish.
Seven golden fish tallies,
cast in gold,
six inches long,
each bearing a character and number.
Each fish was divided into left and right halves that matched.
When there was an affair,
the left half was first given to the defending general,
the envoy held the right half,
and when the size, length, and character numbers matched,
troops would then be dispatched.
Upon completion of the matter,
they were returned to the imperial treasury.
Two hundred silver plates,
one chi (foot) long,
engraved with the national characters,
with the inscription
"Yí Sù" (Urgent Speed),
and also
"Chì Zǒumǎ Pái" (Imperial Galloping Horse Plate).
When the state faced important matters,
the emperor personally bestowed a plate upon an envoy,
and a handwritten note allocated a certain number of relay horses.
If relay horses were lacking,
other horses were used as substitutes.
By law,
they galloped seven hundred li day and night,
or five hundred li for the next fastest.
Wherever they arrived, it was as if the Son of Heaven himself was present;
they could request changes and replacements,
and no one dared to defy them.
Upon the envoy's return,
the emperor personally received it,
and the Pái Yì Lángjūn (Officer in Charge of Plates and Seals) sealed and stored it by hand.
Tàizōng Jìng'ān Empress Xiāo shì,

was the daughter of Chúnqīn Empress's brother Shìshìlǔ.
When the Emperor was Grand Marshal,
she was taken as a consort,
and gave birth to Mùzōng.
Upon his accession,
she was made Empress.
She was intelligent, pure, and simple by nature,
and was especially favored.
Even during military campaigns and hunts, she would always accompany him.
In Tiānxiǎn 10, she passed away,
posthumously named Zhāngdé,
and buried in Fènlíng.
In Chóngxī 21,
her posthumous name was changed to the current one.

was the daughter of Chúnqīn Empress's brother Āgǔzhǐ.
When the Emperor was Prince of Yǒngkāng,
she was taken,

At the end of Tiānlù,
she was made Empress.
In the autumn of the following year,
she gave birth to Princess Ménggǔ.
While she was in confinement,
Chágē rebelled,
assassinating the Empress Dowager and the Emperor.
The Empress rode a litter

her posthumous name was changed to the current one.

She was greatly favored,
and gave birth to Níngwáng Zhǐmò.
Upon his accession,
she was made Empress.

with an elegant demeanor.
She managed the inner palace with rules,
allowing no personal interference.
Liú Zhīyuǎn and Guō Wēi proclaimed themselves emperors,

The Empress participated in the imperial tent,
secretly assisting in grand strategies,
but they were not adopted.
When Chágē rebelled,
she was killed.

the two Empresses were buried on Yīwūlǘ Shān,

Mùzōng Empress Xiāo shì,
whose father Zhīfán,
was a Chamberlain for Court Ceremonials and Hanlin Academician.
When the Empress was born,
auspicious clouds and a fragrant aroma lingered for a long time.
As a child, she had proper deportment.
When the Emperor was a regional prince,
she was taken as a consort.
Upon ascending to the central palace,
she was gentle and compliant by nature,
unable to correct others.
She had no children.

whose given name was Chuò,
and *xiǎozì* Yànyàn,
was the daughter of the Northern Chancellor Sīwēn.

Sīwēn once observed his daughters sweeping the ground,
and only the Empress swept it clean.
He happily said:
"This daughter will surely be able to establish a family!"
Upon the Emperor's accession,
she was chosen as noble consort.
Soon after, she was enfeoffed as Empress,
and gave birth to Shèngzōng.
Upon Jǐngzōng's death,
she was honored as Empress Dowager,
and managed the affairs of the state.
The Empress wept, saying:
"The mother is a widow, the son is weak,
the clan members are powerful,
and the border defenses are not yet settled. What shall we do?"
Yēlǜ Xiézhěn and Hán Dé ràng stepped forward and said:
"If you trust your servants,
what worries are there?"

the Empress, along with Xiézhěn and Dé ràng, deliberated on major state affairs,

she was granted the honorable title of Chéngtiān Empress Dowager.
In Tǒnghé 24,
she was further granted the honorable title of Ruìdé Shénlüè Yìngyùn Qǐhuà Chéngtiān Empress Dowager.

posthumously named Shèngshén Xuānxiàn Empress.
In Chóngxī 21,
her posthumous name was changed to the current one.

always following good advice,
thus all her officials exerted their loyalty.
She was skilled in military administration.
During the Battle of Chányuān,
she personally rode the war chariot,
commanding the three armies.
Rewards and punishments were clear and trustworthy,
and the generals and soldiers fought bravely.
Shèngzōng was called a prosperous ruler of Liáo,
much of which was due to her teachings and guidance.

At the age of twelve,

she was selected into the imperial harem.
In Tǒnghé 19,
she was enfeoffed as Qítiān Empress.

secretly giving it to the relevant officials,

she was even more favored and distinguished.
Her carriage was adorned with dragon heads and *chīwěi*,

each with ingenious designs.
In summer and autumn, she traveled through mountains and valleys,

making people look upon her as a goddess.
She gave birth to two imperial princes,
both of whom died young.

the palace woman Nòujīn gave birth to Xīngzōng,

"Old hag, does your favor have an end?"

Nòujīn enthroned herself as Empress Dowager,

Xīngzōng heard of it and said:
"The Empress served the late Emperor for forty years,
and nurtured my humble self.
She should be Empress Dowager;

but she is also being accused.
Is this acceptable?"
Qīn'āi replied:
"If this person remains,
I fear future troubles."
The Emperor said:
"The Empress has no children and is old.
Even if she remains,
she can do nothing."
Qīn'āi did not agree,
and moved the Empress to Shàngjīng.
When the imperial carriage went on a spring hunt,
Qīn'āi, fearing that the Emperor harbored gratitude for her upbringing,
dispatched someone to harm her.
When the envoy arrived,
the Empress said:
"I am truly innocent,
as the whole world knows.
Sir, please allow me to bathe,
and then I will die.
May I?"
The envoy withdrew.
By the time he returned,
the Empress had already passed away,
at the age of fifty.
On that day,
some people saw the Empress in the shade of Mùyè Shān,
riding a blue-canopied carriage,
with a very strict escort.
She was posthumously honored as Réndé Hòu Huáng.
She was buried together with Qīn'āi in Qìnglíng.

The Emperor appointed Díliè as Qígǔ Yuēlā Xiángwěn,
and Húdù as Sùzhíguān.
When Gé framed his elder brother Ālà,
Húdù secretly assisted him.
People at the time found this disgraceful.
Yēlǜ Yǐxīn was Zhī Běiyuàn Shūmì Shì,
and Húdu’s rank was below Yǐxīn,
so he felt resentful and discontent.
Initially,
Húdu had conspired with Chóngyuán’s son, Nièlǔgǔ, to rebel,
wanting them to act quickly.
When the imperial carriage was hunting at Tàizǐ Shān,
he and Nièlǔgǔ coerced archers and troops to attack the imperial traveling palace.
During the battle,
Nièlǔgǔ was hit by a stray arrow and died,
and the crowd scattered.
At that time, his accomplice, Yēlǜ Sālāzhú, happened to be in the hunting ground.
Hearing of the chaos,
he led hunters to assist.
His partisans said to Húdu and others:
“Our army is numerous.
Taking advantage of their unpreparedness,
if we fight a decisive battle in the middle of the night,
the matter might succeed;
but if we wait until tomorrow,
who will follow us?”
Húdu said:
“In a rush,
black and white cannot be distinguished.
If the inner and outer armies respond to each other,
then our cause will be lost.
What delay is there in departing at dawn!”
Chóngyuán listened to Húdu’s plan
and ordered patrols on all sides to wait for dawn.
That night,
the accomplices enthroned Chóngyuán with a usurped title,
and Húdu appointed himself Shūmì Shǐ.
The next day, they were defeated in battle.
Húdu was wounded
and fled on a single horse.
Upon reaching Shíqī Luò,
he drowned himself.
His five sons
were executed on the same day.
Xiāo Diélǐdé,
courtesy name Húdujǐn,
was a descendant of the maternal uncle’s young father’s branch.
His father, Shuānggǔ,
married Princess Diànnì
and rose to the position of Guójìu Xiángwěn.
Your subject, Tuòtuō, reverently and sincerely bows his head.
I respectfully consider Your Imperial Majesty,
who like Yáo, investigates antiquity,
and is broad-minded and accommodating of the multitude;
who like Shùn, loves to inquire,
and whose profound wisdom surpasses all others.
You lecture on the classics while also reciting ancestral precepts,
and in seeking good governance, you extensively consult past records.
Now, this project of compiling history
is decided by Your Imperial heart.
As Your sagacious decree descended, invitations were issued,
court officials congratulated, and forgotten talents emerged.
Thereupon, Your subject Tuòtuō was appointed as Chancellor of the Right of the Central Secretariat, leading as Chief Compiler-in-Chief.

From the Central Secretariat, Confucian scholars and respected eunuchs were selected: Liánhuì Shānhǎiyá, now Minister of War; Wáng Yí, Hanlin Academician; Xú Bǐng, Editor of the Secretariat; Chén Yìzēng, Compiler of the National History Institute, were assigned to compile the History of the Liáo Dynasty.
The work began in the fourth month of the third year of Zhìzhèng,
and concluded in the third month of the fourth year.
From the stored archives of the old imperial library,
and from tributes offered by distant regions,
materials were collected and sifted through,
then edited, refined, and polished.
Annals, Treatises, Tables, and Biographies
were fully compiled into a history of an era;
evaluations of good and bad, right and wrong,
ensure that the truths of a thousand years are not obscured.
Your subject Tuòtuō, having been entrusted with this great responsibility,
is fortunate to witness its completion.
May it proclaim the splendor of the sun and moon,
and may this small effort contribute to Your Majesty's glory.
The discussions of our dynasty are now rightly guided,
for when the spirit is upright, the words flourish;
should the rulers and ministers of the Liáo state possess awareness,
the good among them will rejoice, and the wicked will fear.
The work comprises thirty volumes of Annals, thirty-two volumes of Treatises,
eight volumes of Tables, and forty-six volumes of Biographies,
each with critical essays and eulogies,
fully embodying the established style,
and is herewith presented along with the tables.
May it ascend to Your Heavenly gaze.
Your humble servant's feelings are overwhelmed with shame, fear, trembling, and apprehension.
Your subject Tuòtuō reverently, sincerely, and humbly bows his head, bowing again and again, respectfully submitting this.

General Principles for the Three Histories
1. Imperial Annals: For the writing style of the annals of the Three Dynasties,
we follow the Shǐjì, Xī Hànshū, and Xīn Tángshū.
For titles and other matters concerning the various states,
we follow the Nánshǐ and Běishǐ.
1. Treatises: From the contents recorded in the various histories,
we select the most important ones to form the treatises.
1. Tables: Tables are similar to treatises.
1. Biographies: Empresses and Consorts,
Imperial Clan,
Imperial Relatives by Marriage,
Ministers,
and Miscellaneous Biographies.
For those subjects who rendered great service,
even if father and son, each receives a separate biography.
Others are grouped by category,
or several individuals share one biography.
Matters recorded in the Three Histories that relate to our present dynasty
should be reported.
Ministers who died for the Jīn and Sòng dynasties
should all have biographies,
without needing to avoid any taboos.
For other matters that cannot be fully included,
the Chief Compilers and Compiling Officials will deliberate in detail when drafting the text.
1. Doubtful matters are recorded as doubtful,
and credible matters are recorded as credible,
following the Chūnqiū.
